1.note: The author is saying **every** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. The leaders of the various Israelite tribes also commanded the soldiers from those tribes. While David did not necessarily speak with every single tribal leader in Israel, it seems he was careful to speak with leaders from every tribe. Alternate translation: [with leaders from every tribe]

2.note: While the expression **the assembly of Israel** can sometimes describe all of the Israelites, in this context it refers to their representatives, the leaders whom the author describes in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [to all of those leaders]

David is using a common expression of his culture to mean “If it seems good to you” or “If you approve.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If it seems good to you] or [If you approve]

David is using a common expression of his culture to mean “and it is the will of Yahweh our God” or “and something that Yahweh our God is leading us to do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it is the will of Yahweh our God] or [and something that Yahweh our God is leading us to do]

David is saying what he wants to do together with the Israelite leaders. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech, and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in such contexts what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire for us to break through, I desire for us to send] or [we should break through, we should send]

David is using **let us break through** as a common expression of his culture to mean “let us act quickly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is high time for us to send] or [let us act quickly and send]
See how you translated the term “brothers” in 6:39. Alternate translation: [our kinsmen who are not here] or [our fellow Israelites who are not here]

The expression **be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let them gather to us] or [and let us gather them to us]

3.q: וְ⁠נָסֵ֛בָּה אֶת־אֲר֥וֹן אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ אֵלֵ֑י⁠נוּ כִּי־לֹ֥א דְרַשְׁנֻ֖⁠הוּ בִּ⁠ימֵ֥י שָׁאֽוּל
3.note: David is giving an implied reason why the Israelites should bring **the Box** to Jerusalem. You could indicate this reason explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And let us bring the Box of our God back to us so that we can seek it, as we did not do in the days of Saul]

3.q: וְ⁠נָסֵ֛בָּה אֶת־אֲר֥וֹן אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ אֵלֵ֑י⁠נוּ כִּי־לֹ֥א דְרַשְׁנֻ֖⁠הוּ בִּ⁠ימֵ֥י שָׁאֽוּל
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the implied reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And so that we can seek the Box of our God, as we did not do in the days of Saul, let us bring back to us]
By **we**, David means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.
This could mean: (1) Alternate translation: [we did not use it to seek his guidance] or (2) Alternate translation: [we did not take care of it]

David is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time when **Saul** was king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during the reign of Saul]

4.q: וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֥וּ כָֽל־הַ⁠קָּהָ֖ל לַ⁠עֲשׂ֣וֹת כֵּ֑ן כִּֽי־יָשַׁ֥ר הַ⁠דָּבָ֖ר בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י כָל־הָ⁠עָֽם
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since the matter was right in the eyes of all of the people, all of the assembly said to do thus]

The author is using the term **eyes** to mean “perspective” and “judgment.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the judgment of all of the people] or [from the perspective of all of the people]

5.note: See how you translated the term “Israel” in 2:7. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

The author is referring to all of the territory of Israel by naming locations at two extremes, **Shihor** in the far south and **Lebo Hamath** in the far north. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from throughout the nation’s territory]

6.note: Marking travel for change in elevation, the author says **went up** because Kiriath Jearim was higher than Hebron. He says **bring up** because Jerusalem, where David wanted to bring the Box, was higher than Kiriath Jearim. See how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [And David went … to bring]

The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the city he calls **Baalah**, its name at this time, is the one they now know as **Kiriath Jearim**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

6.q: אֵת֩ אֲר֨וֹן הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֧ים ׀ יְהוָ֛ה יוֹשֵׁ֥ב הַ⁠כְּרוּבִ֖ים אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שֵֽׁם
6.note: The expression **is called** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Box that people call by the name of God, Yahweh, sitter of the cherubs]

7.note: The author assumes that readers will know, as the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 6:3 indicates, that **Uzzah** and **Ahio** were the sons of **Abinadab**. You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

The author is speaking of **the cart** to mean the oxen that were pulling the cart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the oxen that were pulling the cart]

8.note: The author is saying **all** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and all of the Israelites who were present]
To translate this expression here and in verse 10, see how you translated the similar expression in 11:3. Alternate translation: [in the presence of God]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [with great might]

The term **tambourines** describes hand-held drums with metal discs around their frames that jingle when people shake or strike the drums. If your readers would not be familiar with what a tambourine is, you could use the name of a similar instrument that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and with hand drums] or [and with jingling drums]

9.note: The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 6:6 reads “Nacon.” Scholars are not certain which name is more likely original, so we recommend that you do not try to use the same name in both of these places in your translation. It is possible that both names are a development of some earlier form.

9.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֨ח עֻזָּ֜א אֶת־יָד֗⁠וֹ לֶ⁠אֱחֹז֙ אֶת־הָ֣⁠אָר֔וֹן כִּ֥י שָֽׁמְט֖וּ הַ⁠בָּקָֽר
9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because the oxen stumbled, Uzzah stretched out his hand to hold the Box]

10.note: The author is describing Yahweh becoming extremely angry by alluding to the way a person’s **nose** may become hot and red when he is angry. Your culture may also associate anger with heat or with a particular part of the body, and if so, you could use its characteristic expression in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh blazed with fury] or [And Yahweh became extremely angry]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because he had stretched out his hand upon the Box, he struck him]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [And David became very angry]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.
The name **Perez Uzzah** means “Outbreak against Uzzah.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and that is still its name to this day]
See the discussion of the phrase **to this day** in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and that is still its name as of the time of this writing]

12.q: הֵ֚יךְ אָבִ֣יא אֵלַ֔⁠י אֵ֖ת אֲר֥וֹן הָ⁠אֱלֹהִֽים
12.note: David is using the question form to express his concern about trying bring the Box of Yahweh to where he lives. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I should not dare to try to bring the Box of God to me!]

13.note: Here the author is introducing **Obed Edom** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain man named Obed Edom who came from Gath]

14.note: The author is using the term **house** in the first and third instances to mean the people who lived in the same house with **Obed Edom**, that is, his extended family or his household. (The term is literal in the second instance.) If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the household of Obed Edom … the household of Obed Edom]
